spot.title: Tunnelling through a 1 eV barrier
spot.intro: An electron ($m_e$) with $E$ below a rectangular barrier of height $V_0$ and width $a$, $V_0-E=1\,\mathrm{eV}$, $a=0.5\,\mathrm{nm}$. Estimate the transmission. One step is wrong.
steps: Inside the barrier $\psi''=\kappa^2\psi$ with $\kappa>0$ real, since $E<V_0$.
Hence $\kappa a\approx 2.56\gg 1$, so the thick-barrier approximation applies.
spot.why: The transmission probability is $|t|^2$, and the amplitude inside the barrier decays as $e^{-\kappa a}$. The probability therefore decays with the square of that factor, $e^{-2\kappa a}$. Using $e^{-\kappa a}$ overestimates $T$ by more than an order of magnitude.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 3 (simple systems/tunnelling) and the tunnelling sheets, topic T ~ e^{-2 kappa a}

spot.title: Position variance in the state $|n\rangle$
spot.intro: Compute $\langle x^2\rangle$ in the oscillator eigenstate $|n\rangle$ with ladder operators. One step contains an error.
steps: $\langle n|a^2|n\rangle=\langle n|a^{\dagger2}|n\rangle=0$ since they change $n$ by $\pm2$.
spot.why: The two surviving terms must be added, not subtracted: both $aa^\dagger$ and $a^\dagger a$ appear with a plus sign in $x^2$. The subtraction would make $\langle x^2\rangle$ independent of $n$, which contradicts the growing classical amplitude.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 6 (harmonic oscillator), topic ladder-operator expectation values

spot.title: The commutator $[L_x,L_y]$
spot.intro: Derive $[L_x,L_y]$ from $L_x=yp_z-zp_y$, $L_y=zp_x-xp_z$ and $[x_i,p_j]=i\hbar\delta_{ij}$. One step is wrong.
steps: $[yp_z,xp_z]=[zp_y,zp_x]=0$ because the operators involved all commute.
spot.why: The sum is $i\hbar(xp_y-yp_x)$, and $L_z=xp_y-yp_x$. Writing $yp_x-xp_y$ is $-L_z$, so the claimed identification with $L_z$ has the wrong sign (it would flip the orientation of the algebra).

source.where: adapted from script ch. 7 (angular momentum), topic commutation relations of L

spot.title: First-order shift: half-filled box
spot.intro: Infinite well $0<x<L$, $\psi_1=\sqrt{2/L}\sin(\pi x/L)$. Perturbation $H'=V_0$ for $0<x<L/2$ and $0$ elsewhere. Find $E_1^{(1)}$. One step is wrong.
steps: $\int_0^{L/2}\sin^2(\pi x/L)\,dx=\tfrac L2$, since the integral of $\sin^2$ over a half period is the full-box value.
spot.why: The cosine term gives $\sin(2\pi x/L)\big|_0^{L/2}=0$, so the integral is $\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac L2=\tfrac L4$. The value $L/2$ is the integral over the whole box $0..L$. The result $E_1^{(1)}=V_0$ is also impossible: perturbing only half of the box must shift the energy by less than $V_0$.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 11 (perturbation theory), topic first-order shift in the infinite well

spot.title: Probabilities of a non-normalised spinor
spot.intro: A spin-1/2 particle is prepared in $|\psi\rangle=|{\uparrow}\rangle+(1+i)|{\downarrow}\rangle$ (eigenstates of $S_z$). Find $P(\uparrow)$ and $\langle S_z\rangle$. One step is wrong.
spot.why: A probability is the squared modulus of the amplitude. The amplitude is $1/\sqrt3$, so $P(\uparrow)=1/3$. The values $1/\sqrt3$ and $2/3$ do not even add up to 1, which is a quick check that catches this error.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 4 (formalism), topic Born rule with normalisation

spot.title: Wavelength of the Balmer-$\alpha$ line
spot.intro: Compute the wavelength of the hydrogen transition $n=3\to n=2$ with $E_n=-13.6\,\mathrm{eV}/n^2$. One step is wrong.
spot.why: From $\hbar\omega=\Delta E$ and $\omega=2\pi c/\lambda$ one gets $\lambda=2\pi\hbar c/\Delta E=hc/\Delta E$. Using $\hbar c$ instead of $hc$ drops a factor $2\pi$ (h versus hbar mix-up). The result 104 nm would be in the UV, but Balmer-$\alpha$ is the red line.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 8 (hydrogen), topic Rydberg spectrum, Balmer series

spot.title: Hydrogen ground state from the uncertainty principle
spot.intro: Estimate the ground-state energy: take $p\sim\hbar/r$ and minimise $E(r)=\frac{p^2}{2m}-\frac{e^2}{r}$ (Gaussian units, $a=\hbar^2/me^2$). One step is wrong.
spot.why: The derivative of $\hbar^2/(2mr^2)$ is $-\hbar^2/(mr^3)$: the factor 2 from the power cancels the 2 in the denominator. The wrong factor leads to a vanishing energy, in contradiction with the existence of a bound state.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 4/8, topic uncertainty-principle estimate of the hydrogen ground state

spot.title: Building the triplet state $|1,0\rangle$
spot.intro: Two spin-1/2 particles. Starting from $|1,1\rangle=|{\uparrow\uparrow}\rangle$ construct $|1,0\rangle$ with the lowering operator. One step is wrong.
steps: The singlet is orthogonal to it: $|0,0\rangle=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\big(|{\uparrow\downarrow}\rangle-|{\downarrow\uparrow}\rangle\big)$.
spot.why: Dividing $\hbar(|{\downarrow\uparrow}\rangle+|{\uparrow\downarrow}\rangle)$ by $\sqrt2\hbar$ gives a prefactor $1/\sqrt2$, not $1/2$. With $1/2$ the state has norm $1/\sqrt2$, so it is not normalised.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 9 (spin addition), topic Clebsch-Gordan via lowering operator

spot.title: Is one half of a singlet pure?
spot.intro: Two qubits in the singlet $|\psi\rangle=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(|{\uparrow\downarrow}\rangle-|{\downarrow\uparrow}\rangle)$. Characterise the state of qubit A alone. One step is wrong.
steps: Trace over B: the cross terms carry $\langle{\uparrow}|{\downarrow}\rangle_B=0$ and drop out.
$\mathrm{Tr}\,\rho_A^2=1$, so qubit A is in a pure state.
spot.why: For $\rho_A=\mathbb 1/2$ one finds $\mathrm{Tr}\rho_A^2=2\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac12<1$, so A is in a maximally mixed state. A global pure state that is entangled always has mixed subsystems.
spot.fix: $\mathrm{Tr}\,\rho_A^2=\tfrac12<1$: A is maximally mixed, with entropy $S=\ln2$.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 10 (entanglement), topic reduced density matrix of the singlet

spot.title: Heisenberg equation for the free particle
spot.intro: Show $\frac d{dt}\langle x\rangle=\langle p\rangle/m$ for $H=p^2/2m$ using $\frac d{dt}\langle x\rangle=\frac i\hbar\langle[H,x]\rangle$. One step is wrong.
spot.why: The canonical commutator is $[x,p]=i\hbar$, so $[p,x]=-i\hbar$. With the order reversed the sign flips and the velocity comes out opposite to the momentum.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 2/4, topic Ehrenfest theorem and Heisenberg equation

limits.title: Doubling the barrier width
limits.prompt: A barrier with $\kappa a\gg1$ has transmission $T_1$. The width is doubled at fixed $V_0-E$. What is the new transmission?
options: $T\approx T_1$, since the exponent is independent of $a$
limits.explain: The exponent is linear in $a$, so doubling $a$ doubles $2\kappa a$ and squares the exponential: $e^{-4\kappa a}=(e^{-2\kappa a})^2$. Tunnelling currents therefore depend exponentially on distance, which is why an STM tip resolves single atoms.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 3, tunnelling

limits.title: Transmission far above the barrier
limits.prompt: What happens to $T$ for a rectangular barrier as $E/V_0\to\infty$?
options: $T\to1$, with $T=1$ exactly at $k'a=n\pi$ below that limit
$T\to0$, because the barrier reflects more at high energy
limits.explain: The correction term scales like $V_0^2/(4E^2)\to0$, so $T\to1$: the barrier becomes a small perturbation. At finite $E>V_0$ the transmission is below 1 except at the resonances $k'a=n\pi$, where the reflected waves from the two edges cancel.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 3, scattering from a barrier

limits.title: Classical limit of tunnelling
limits.prompt: What happens to the tunnelling probability in the limit $\hbar\to0$ at fixed $m$, $a$, $V_0-E>0$?
options: $T$ stays finite, because tunnelling is a wave effect
limits.explain: $\kappa\propto1/\hbar$ diverges, so the exponent goes to $-\infty$ and $T\to0$. The same happens for macroscopic $m$ or $a$: a ball does not tunnel through a wall.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 3, tunnelling and correspondence

limits.title: Large-$n$ oscillator density
limits.prompt: For large $n$ the locally averaged probability density $|\psi_n(x)|^2$ of the harmonic oscillator approaches the classical one. Where is the classical probability largest?
options: At the centre $x=0$, where the particle is fastest
At the turning points $x=\pm A$, where the particle is slowest
limits.explain: The classical density is $\propto1/v(x)\propto1/\sqrt{A^2-x^2}$, which diverges at the turning points where the velocity vanishes. The quantum density oscillates fast, with the envelope following this form (correspondence principle), unlike the ground state which peaks at $x=0$.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 6, correspondence principle

limits.title: Stiffening the oscillator
limits.prompt: The spring constant is increased so that $\omega\to\infty$. What happens to the ground-state width and energy?
options: Width $\to0$ and $E_0\to0$, as for a classical particle at rest
limits.explain: The width $\propto\omega^{-1/2}$ shrinks, so confinement raises the kinetic energy. The zero-point energy $\hbar\omega/2$ grows linearly in $\omega$. A classical particle could sit at rest at the bottom with $E=0$, but this would violate $\Delta x\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 6, zero-point energy

limits.title: Large-$n$ hydrogen transitions
limits.prompt: For $n\gg1$, how does the frequency of the $n\to n-1$ transition scale?
limits.explain: Expanding gives $\tfrac1{(n-1)^2}-\tfrac1{n^2}\approx2/n^3$. Classically $\omega_{orb}\propto r^{-3/2}$ with $r\propto n^2$, i.e. $\propto n^{-3}$. This is Bohr's correspondence principle for hydrogen.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 8, hydrogen spectrum

limits.title: Positronium binding energy
limits.prompt: Replace the proton by a positron (equal mass $m_e$, charge $+e$). How does the ground-state binding energy compare to hydrogen?
options: It is the same, because only the charge enters
It is zero, since particle and antiparticle annihilate
limits.explain: The energy scale is set by the reduced mass. For hydrogen $\mu\approx m_e$; for equal masses $\mu=m_e/2$, so all binding energies halve and the Bohr radius doubles. Annihilation only limits the lifetime, not the level scheme.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 8, reduced mass

limits.title: Strong-field Zeeman effect
limits.prompt: In the limit $B\to\infty$ (Paschen-Back), which are the good quantum numbers and what is the energy shift?
limits.explain: When the Zeeman term dominates over spin-orbit coupling, $L_z$ and $S_z$ are conserved separately and the first-order shift is $\mu_BB(m_l+2m_s)$. The Landé form $g_J\mu_Bm_jB$ only holds for weak fields ($B\to0$), where $\vec L\cdot\vec S$ dominates.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 8/11, Zeeman effect

limits.title: Sign of the second-order shift
limits.prompt: What is the sign of the second-order correction to the ground-state energy for any perturbation $H'$?
options: It depends on the sign of $H'$
Zero, since first order already gives the exact shift
limits.explain: All numerators are non-negative and all denominators $E_0-E_m$ are negative for the ground state, so $E_0^{(2)}\le0$ whatever the sign of $H'$: level repulsion pushes the ground state down. This also agrees with the variational bound.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 11, perturbation theory

limits.title: Large-$l$ angular momentum
limits.prompt: What happens to the relative spacing $\Delta L_z/|\vec L|$ of the allowed $L_z$ values for $l\to\infty$?
options: It tends to 0, so $\vec L$ can point in any direction (classical limit)
limits.explain: Neighbouring $m$ values differ by $\hbar$, so $\Delta L_z/|\vec L|=1/\sqrt{l(l+1)}\to0$. The discrete orientations merge into a continuum, as required by the correspondence principle.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 7, angular momentum

limits.title: Box of growing width
limits.prompt: What happens to the level spacing $E_{n+1}-E_n$ of the infinite well as $L\to\infty$?
options: It tends to 0 as $1/L^2$, giving a continuum of free-particle states
limits.explain: The spacing is $\pi^2\hbar^2(2n+1)/(2mL^2)\to0$. The levels become dense, and the standing waves turn into a continuous free-particle spectrum $E=\hbar^2k^2/2m$.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 3, infinite well

limits.title: Very shallow 1D well
limits.prompt: How many bound states does a 1D symmetric well have in the limit $V_0\to0$ at fixed width?
options: None; a minimum depth is needed
Exactly one, with binding energy $\propto V_0^2$
Exactly one, with binding energy $\propto V_0$
limits.explain: In one dimension every attractive well has at least one even bound state. For $V_0\to0$ it is very extended, $\kappa\propto V_0$, so the binding energy $\propto\kappa^2\propto V_0^2$. The depth threshold exists only in 3D.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 3, finite well

limits.title: Long-time spreading
limits.prompt: How does the width of a free Gaussian packet behave for $t\to\infty$?
options: It approaches a constant, set by $\Delta x_0$
It grows linearly, $\Delta x\to\hbar t/(2m\Delta x_0)$, so a narrower initial packet spreads faster
It shrinks again after the packet reaches its focus
limits.explain: For large $t$ the second term dominates and $\Delta x\to\hbar t/(2m\Delta x_0)$. A small $\Delta x_0$ means a large $\Delta p$, so faster spreading. The momentum spread $\Delta p$ does not change in free evolution.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 2/4, free wave packet

limits.title: Singlet correlations at 90 degrees
limits.prompt: Alice measures along $z$, Bob along $x$ on a singlet. What is the correlation $E=\langle\sigma_z\otimes\sigma_x\rangle$?
options: $0$: Bob's outcome is statistically independent of Alice's
limits.explain: The correlation is $-\cos\theta$ with $\theta=90^\circ$, which vanishes: each outcome is $\pm1$ with probability $1/2$ independent of the other. Perfect anticorrelation holds only for parallel axes.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 10, entanglement

limits.title: Landé factor for $L=0$
limits.prompt: What is $g_J$ for a state with $l=0$ ($j=s=\tfrac12$)?
limits.explain: With $l=0$: $g_J=1+\frac{3/4+3/4}{2\cdot3/4}=2$. For pure orbital angular momentum ($s=0$) one gets 1 instead, so $g_J$ interpolates between the orbital and the spin $g$-factor.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 9, Landé factor

sketch.title: Probability densities in the infinite well
sketch.task: Sketch $|\psi_n(x)|^2$ for $n=1,2,3$ in the infinite well $0<x<L$.
features: $|\psi_n|^2$ vanishes at both walls, $x=0$ and $x=L$.
$n$ maxima, each of height $2/L$.
$n-1$ interior nodes at $x=kL/n$.
All curves are symmetric or antisymmetric about $L/2$ (the density is always symmetric).
sketch.tips: Every curve has the same area 1.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 3, topic infinite well eigenfunctions

sketch.title: Transmission across a rectangular barrier
sketch.task: Sketch the transmission $T$ as a function of $E/V_0$ for a rectangular barrier with $\sqrt{2mV_0}\,a/\hbar=4$.
features: $T\to0$ as $E\to0$, exponentially small ($\sim e^{-2\kappa a}$).
$T$ is smooth through $E=V_0$, with $T=1/(1+g^2/4)=0.2$ there for $g=4$.
For $E>V_0$, $T$ oscillates and reaches $1$ at the resonances $k'a=n\pi$.
The oscillation minima rise towards $1$ as $E/V_0\to\infty$.
sketch.tips: Here g = sqrt(2 m V0) a / hbar.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 3, topic rectangular barrier transmission

sketch.title: Radial probability densities of hydrogen n=2
sketch.task: Sketch the radial probability density $P(r)=r^2R_{nl}(r)^2$ for the $2s$ and $2p$ states of hydrogen as a function of $r/a$.
features: 2s has a node at $r=2a$ and two maxima, at $r\approx0.76a$ and $r\approx5.2a$.
2p has no node and a single maximum at $r=4a$ (Bohr radius of $n=2$).
$P\propto r^2$ for 2s but $\propto r^4$ for 2p near the origin: the centrifugal barrier suppresses 2p at small $r$.
Both curves decay as $e^{-r/a}$ and each integrates to 1.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 8, topic hydrogen radial wave functions R20 and R21

sketch.title: Normal Zeeman splitting of the 2p level
sketch.task: Sketch the energy shift of the $l=1$ level (spin neglected) as a function of $B$ for $m=-1,0,+1$.
features: All three levels start at the same energy at $B=0$ (threefold degeneracy).
$E=m\mu_BB$: straight lines with slopes $+\mu_B,0,-\mu_B$.
Equidistant splitting $\mu_BB\approx58\,\mu\mathrm{eV}$ per tesla.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 8/11, topic Zeeman effect, first-order perturbation theory

sketch.title: Finite square well and its ground state
sketch.task: Sketch the potential $V(x)$ of a finite square well of half-width $a$ and depth $V_0$, and the ground-state wave function, drawn at its energy level (here $\sqrt{2mV_0}\,a/\hbar=3$).
features: The ground state is even and nodeless, with its energy $E_0>0$ above the well floor and below $V_0$.
Inside, $\psi\propto\cos kx$ with $k<\pi/2a$, so the curve is rounder than in the infinite well.
Outside, $\psi$ decays exponentially (evanescent tail), with a continuous slope at $x=\pm a$.
The wave function penetrates into the classically forbidden region; the tail is the reason $E_0$ is lower than the infinite-well value.
sketch.tips: The baseline of psi is drawn at E/V0; the amplitude scale is arbitrary.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 3, topic finite potential well

sketch.title: Spreading of a free Gaussian wave packet
sketch.task: Sketch the width $\Delta x(t)/\Delta x_0$ of a free Gaussian packet as a function of $t/t_s$, $t_s=2m\Delta x_0^2/\hbar$, and add its late-time asymptote.
features: Starts at $\Delta x(0)/\Delta x_0=1$ with zero slope (parabolic start).
At $t=t_s$ the width is $\sqrt2\,\Delta x_0$.
Late times: linear growth $\Delta x\to\Delta x_0\,t/t_s$, i.e. the asymptote.
The curve lies above the asymptote everywhere and approaches it from above.

source.where: adapted from script ch. 2/4, topic free particle Gaussian wave packet
